anatomy.lede: The nautilus is a cephalopod in a coiled house: a soft, many-armed body living in the last and largest room of a shell it keeps adding to.

hotspots.label: Hood
hotspots.text: The tough, spotted hood works like a trapdoor. When the animal pulls back into its shell, the hood seals the opening.

hotspots.label: Pinhole eye
hotspots.text: The eye has no lens and works like a pinhole. It can sense only light and dark.

hotspots.label: Tentacles
hotspots.text: More than 90 suckerless tentacles feel, taste and grip. They are ridged and coated in a sticky secretion that holds prey.

hotspots.label: Striped shell
hotspots.text: Young shells are striped, and the stripes stretch as the animal grows. Each nautilus's pattern is distinctive enough to tell individuals apart.

hotspots.label: Living chamber
hotspots.text: The body occupies only the outermost chamber. Behind it, the older chambers hold the gas and liquid that keep the animal afloat.

senses.lede: In the dim deep reef, a nautilus finds food mainly by smell, with simple eyes adding a sense of light and shade.

senses.name: Rhinophores
senses.text: In experiments in the dark, nautiluses followed drifting odour plumes to their source from up to 10 m away. When two small smell organs, the rhinophores, were blocked, they could no longer find the source.

senses.name: Tentacles
senses.text: The thin tentacles can detect odour too, but in the same experiments they did not steer the animal. Instead they taste and touch as it feels along the reef.

senses.name: Pinhole eye
senses.text: The simple, lens-less eyes can only sense light and dark. They seem to play a smaller part than smell in finding food.

body.lede: A nautilus floats, steers and feeds with equipment that has served its ancestors for hundreds of millions of years.

systems.title: Buoyancy control
systems.text: A tube running back through the shell controls how much gas and liquid each chamber holds, letting the animal fine-tune its buoyancy as it rises and sinks.

systems.title: Jet propulsion
systems.text: It swims by squirting water from its mantle cavity through a flexible siphon near the head. Pointing the siphon lets it move forwards, backwards or sideways.

systems.title: Beak and radula
systems.text: Prey held by the tentacles is broken up by a hard, beak-like mouth and then shredded further by a radula, a ribbon lined with tiny teeth.

systems.title: Building the shell
systems.text: The genome contains a conserved molluscan toolkit for making shell, plus repetitive protein sections found only in this lineage, which together build its shell.

genome.lede: Two research teams published nautilus genomes in 2021, giving the first full genetic look at a shelled cephalopod.

findings.title: Compact and slow-changing
findings.text: Compared with other cephalopods, the nautilus genome is compact, has relatively few genes and has evolved slowly.

findings.title: Genes behind the pinhole eye
findings.text: Losses of certain genes, and changes in the size of gene families and their control networks, probably shaped the evolution of the lens-less pinhole eye.

findings.title: Jumping genes
findings.text: A chromosome-level assembly of about 785 million base pairs found recent activity of transposable elements, 'jumping genes' that may have helped the lineage adapt.

mind.lede: The nautilus has fewer brain lobes and neurons than octopuses or squid, yet it can still learn and remember.

studies.title: Light means food
studies.text: Nautiluses learned to link a blue light with the smell of food, and soon stretched out their tentacles at the light alone. Learning appeared within ten trials spread over 30 minutes.

studies.title: Two kinds of memory
studies.text: The trained response lasted under an hour, faded, then returned about six hours after training and lasted up to a day. This two-phase pattern resembles that of cuttlefish.

studies.title: Memory without a memory centre
studies.text: Nautiluses lack the vertical lobe that coleoid cephalopods use for learning, so their memory must rely on other parts of the brain.

survival.lede: With no ink and no colour-changing skin, the nautilus relies on its shell and on staying deep by day.

tactics.title: Retreat and seal
tactics.text: At any threat it can withdraw into its shell and close the hood over the opening.

tactics.title: Daytime refuge
tactics.text: It spends the day on deep reef slopes, away from predators, and rises to feed only at night.

tactics.title: No ink, no disguise
tactics.text: Unlike octopuses and squid, it has no ink sac and cannot camouflage itself, which may make learning to avoid danger especially valuable.

threats.title: Shell trade
threats.text: Overharvesting for souvenirs, jewellery and décor is the main threat. Targeted fishing continues in Indonesia, the Philippines and China despite bans.

threats.title: Slow to recover
threats.text: Because nautiluses mature late and produce few young, fished populations are prone to serious decline.

life.lede: A nautilus grows slowly, adding chamber after chamber over a decade or more before it can breed.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: A female lays only 10 to 18 eggs a year, each about the size and shape of a garlic bulb.

stages.name: Hatchling
stages.text: The young nautilus hatches with a striped shell that already has seven or eight small chambers.

stages.name: Juvenile
stages.text: It keeps adding chambers as it grows, and reaches maturity at around 10 to 15 years old.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: A mature nautilus has about 30 chambers and continues to rise each night to feed and lay eggs.
